Motlanthe will stay in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge threw out the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma -- Mbeki's political arch rival. The judge called the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference. Mbeki -- who has been South Africa's president for nearly 10 years -- spoke of some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation on Sunday during a televised address. Mbeki said the country still has economic, corruption and crime challenges to face in the future. He also faced charges of having a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma's political influence to benefit his businesses. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside the violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under it, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and the coordinator of government affairs.

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have tendered their resignations as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to depart from office. President Mbeki formally announced his resignation in a televised address on Sunday. His successor, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, is scheduled to be sworn in as South Africa's president on Thursday.

Mbeki's announcement on Sunday prompted several Cabinet members to threaten resignation in solidarity; however, the outgoing president urged them to remain in their posts, according to government sources. The resignations—which include those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will take effect on Thursday when Mbeki formally steps down, a government statement said.

"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement noted. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel remains willing to serve in the new government should his services be required. Three deputy ministers have likewise submitted their resignations, according to a government statement.

A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that it had selected Motlanthe as its chosen successor to Mbeki. Motlanthe will hold office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win.

Earlier this month, the ANC called upon Mbeki to step down after a judge dismissed the corruption, fraud, and racketeering case against Zuma—Mbeki's principal political rival. The judge declared the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference.

Mbeki, who has served as South Africa's president for nearly a decade, reflected on several of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation during Sunday's televised address. Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" »

"I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Under his leadership, he noted, the country enjoyed the longest period of sustained economic growth in its history and extended assistance to impoverished citizens on an unprecedented scale.

Mbeki acknowledged that the nation still faces significant economic, corruption, and crime-related challenges in the years ahead. He also expressed his confidence in the country's next leader, though he refrained from naming that individual.

Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced on Saturday that the party—with which Mbeki has been affiliated since his teenage years—had requested that he leave before the conclusion of his term. Mbeki agreed to comply, Mantashe said.

Mantashe explained that the ANC reached its decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country," and so that the ANC movement could remain "stable and unified."

The case against Zuma—who succeeded Mbeki as ANC president last year—was initially dismissed in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority subsequently recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson issued no ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility that he could be recharged. Political observers, however, considered such an outcome unlikely given Zuma's widespread popularity, particularly among the Communist Party and trade unions.

Zuma has consistently denied the charges. He maintained that the case was politically motivated and had undermined his prospects of becoming the ANC's presidential nominee. Had he been convicted of accepting bribes from a company that secured a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, he could have faced a minimum of 15 years in prison. He also faced charges of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is currently serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf and exploiting Zuma's political influence to benefit his own business interests.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics have alleged that he actively pushed for the corruption charges brought against Zuma.

Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the accord on Monday in an effort to move beyond a violent past and resolve the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since the disputed national elections in March. Under the terms of the agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe retains the presidency, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

In a broadcast address on Sunday, the South African leader declared that he was stepping aside. Kgalema Motlanthe, who serves as Deputy President of the African National Congress, has been chosen to succeed him and is scheduled to take the oath of office as the nation's president on Thursday.

According to government sources, once Mbeki revealed his resignation on Sunday, a number of Cabinet officials warned that they intended to quit as well—though the departing president appealed to them to remain in their positions. A government statement noted that the resignations, which involve Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, will become official on Thursday, the same day Mbeki leaves. "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement read. An aide to the finance minister informed CNN that Manuel would be prepared to work within the new government if his services were required. The same government statement indicated that three deputy ministers had also submitted resignations.

A representative for the ANC, the country's governing party, verified that Motlanthe had been selected as its pick to take over from Mbeki. Motlanthe is expected to hold the position through the elections slated for the spring of next year, a contest that ANC President Jacob Zuma is broadly anticipated to win.

Earlier in the month, the ANC requested that Mbeki resign following a judge's dismissal of the corruption, fraud, and racketeering charges leveled against Zuma, who is Mbeki's chief political adversary. The judge deemed the case invalid and charged that Mbeki's administration had meddled politically.

Having served as South Africa's leader for almost a decade, Mbeki referenced several of his accomplishments during his official resignation broadcast on Sunday. "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki stated. He remarked that his tenure had seen the longest stretch of continuous economic expansion in the nation's history, along with an unprecedented effort to assist the poor. Mbeki acknowledged that difficulties involving the economy, corruption, and crime still lay ahead for the country. Without identifying the individual, he expressed his confidence in whoever would become the country's next leader.

On Saturday, Gwede Mantashe, the ANC's secretary-general, disclosed that the party—an organization Mbeki has belonged to since his adolescence—had requested that he depart ahead of the end of his term, a request Mbeki accepted. Mantashe explained that the ANC reached this decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country" and to keep the ANC movement "stable and unified."

The charges against Zuma, who took over from Mbeki as ANC president the previous year, had been dismissed in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority later reinstated them. Judge Chris Nicholson issued no verdict regarding Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility that Zuma could face charges again. Given Zuma's widespread support—especially among the Communist Party and labor unions—political analysts considered a fresh prosecution unlikely.

Zuma has rejected the accusations, describing the case as politically driven and damaging to his prospects of securing the ANC's presidential nomination. Had he been convicted of taking bribes from a firm that secured a contract within a multibillion-dollar arms transaction, he could have received a sentence of at least 15 years. He also confronted allegations of maintaining a corrupt association with Schabir Shaik, his one-time financial adviser, who is currently serving a 15-year term for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf and exploiting Zuma's political clout to advance his own business interests.

Mbeki, aged 66, took over from Nelson Mandela as the country's president in June 1999. His detractors claimed that he had driven the corruption case brought against Zuma. Recently, Mbeki helped negotiate a power-sharing arrangement between Zimbabwe's rival political factions, who put their signatures to the deal on Monday in a bid to move beyond their violent history and resolve the crisis that has gripped Zimbabwe since the contested national elections held in March. Under the terms of the accord, veteran Zimbabwean ruler Robert Mugabe stays on as president, while his long-standing opponent, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister and oversees government affairs.

# Johannesburg, South Africa

Johannesburg, often affectionately called "Jo'burg" or "Jozi," stands as the largest city in South Africa and one of the most vibrant urban centers on the African continent. Located in the northeastern part of the country within the Gauteng province, this bustling metropolis serves as the economic heartbeat of South Africa.

## A City Born from Gold

Johannesburg's origins trace back to 1886, when gold was discovered in the Witwatersrand region. This discovery transformed a modest settlement into a booming mining town almost overnight. Within a few years, it grew into one of the fastest-developing cities in the world, attracting fortune-seekers from across the globe. Today, the legacy of gold mining remains embedded in the city's identity and history.

## Economic Powerhouse

As the financial capital of South Africa, Johannesburg contributes significantly to the nation's economy. The city hosts the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest stock exchange in Africa, along with countless corporate headquarters, banks, and businesses. Its economic influence extends well beyond South Africa's borders, making it a key player in the broader African economy.

## Culture and Diversity

Johannesburg is a melting pot of cultures, languages, and traditions. People from various ethnic backgrounds and nations call this city home, creating a rich tapestry of cultural diversity. Visitors can explore important historical sites such as the Apartheid Museum, which tells the powerful story of South Africa's struggle for freedom and equality, and Constitution Hill.

## Nearby Attractions

The region surrounding Johannesburg offers remarkable experiences. Soweto, a historically significant township, played a crucial role in the anti-apartheid movement and is home to the former residence of Nelson Mandela. Additionally, the nearby Cradle of Humankind, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contains some of the oldest human fossils ever discovered.

## Conclusion

Johannesburg is a city of contrasts and resilience, where history and modernity coexist. From its golden beginnings to its status as a thriving economic hub, Jo'burg continues to shine as a symbol of opportunity and progress in South Africa and across the African continent.

# South African President Thabo Mbeki Resigns Amid Political Turmoil

**Cabinet exodus follows as deputy president and ten ministers step down**

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa — South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation Sunday, bowing to pressure from his own ruling African National Congress (ANC) party after nearly a decade in office.

Mbeki's departure triggered a wave of resignations across his government, with Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and ten cabinet ministers announcing they would also step down from their posts.

## A Party Divided

The resignation comes just days after the ANC's National Executive Committee formally requested that Mbeki step aside, following a bruising internal power struggle with party leader Jacob Zuma.

The conflict between the two men had deepened divisions within the ANC, the party that has governed South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994.

In a televised address to the nation, Mbeki maintained his composure while announcing his decision.

"I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 52 years," Mbeki said. "I remain a member of the ANC and therefore respect its decisions."

## The Court Ruling That Sparked the Crisis

The political drama intensified after a High Court judge suggested there may have been political interference in corruption charges brought against Zuma. The ruling was seen by Zuma's supporters as vindication and increased pressure on Mbeki's leadership.

Zuma had previously defeated Mbeki in a contest for the ANC presidency, setting the stage for the eventual leadership showdown.

## Ministers Follow

Among those tendering their resignations were several senior figures in Mbeki's administration. The mass departure raised concerns about continuity in government during the transition period.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, widely respected in international markets, was among those who initially offered to resign, sparking fears about economic stability. Officials later moved to reassure markets and the public about the country's economic direction.

## What Happens Next

Under South Africa's constitution, the National Assembly is expected to select an interim president to serve until national elections scheduled for 2009.

The ANC's parliamentary majority means the party will effectively choose Mbeki's successor to lead the country through the transition.

Political analysts noted that despite the upheaval, South Africa's democratic institutions remained intact throughout the crisis.

## A Complicated Legacy

Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, presided over a period of significant economic growth. However, his presidency was marked by controversy, including his widely criticized stance on HIV/AIDS and his approach to the political crisis in neighboring Zimbabwe.

The transition marks a significant moment for Africa's largest economy as the nation navigates the political uncertainty ahead.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Mbeki Resigns as South African President; Motlanthe Named Successor Amid Zuma Power Struggle

## ANC Leadership Rift Culminates in Presidential Departure

**JOHANNESBURG** — Thabo Mbeki stepped down as President of South Africa, bringing an abrupt end to a presidency that had guided the nation through nearly a decade of economic growth but ultimately fell victim to a bitter power struggle within the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Mbeki's resignation followed a decision by the ANC's National Executive Committee to "recall" him from office—an unprecedented move that reflected the deep divisions that had fractured the party since Jacob Zuma defeated Mbeki for the ANC presidency at the party's conference in Polokwane in December 2007.

In a televised address to the nation, Mbeki maintained his composure while acknowledging the party's decision, insisting he had served the country to the best of his ability and denying wrongdoing in the controversies that surrounded his final months in office.

## The Judicial Trigger

The immediate catalyst for Mbeki's downfall stemmed from a judgment by Judge Chris Nicholson of the Pietermaritzburg High Court. The ruling dismissed corruption charges against Zuma on procedural grounds and, controversially, suggested there may have been political interference in the National Prosecuting Authority's handling of the case.

The judge's remarks implied that Mbeki's administration may have influenced the decision to prosecute Zuma, a suggestion that provided Zuma's allies within the ANC with the political ammunition needed to demand Mbeki's removal. Mbeki has consistently denied interfering in the prosecution.

## Kgalema Motlanthe Steps In

To fill the vacancy, the ANC nominated **Kgalema Motlanthe**, the party's deputy president and a respected veteran of the anti-apartheid struggle, to serve as caretaker president until national elections.

Motlanthe, a former trade unionist and political prisoner on Robben Island, was widely regarded as a steady, unifying figure. His appointment was intended to reassure both markets and the international community that South Africa's constitutional order remained intact and that the transition would proceed smoothly.

Analysts noted that Motlanthe's role was understood to be transitional, with Zuma positioned as the ANC's presidential candidate for the upcoming general elections.

## The Zuma-Mbeki Rivalry

The events represented the climax of a long-running feud between the two men. Zuma had served as Mbeki's deputy president before being dismissed in 2005 after his financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption in connection with an arms deal. That dismissal set the stage for a protracted battle for control of the ANC.

Zuma's supporters—including the ANC Youth League, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), and the South African Communist Party—rallied behind him, framing his legal troubles as a politically motivated campaign orchestrated by Mbeki's camp.

## Reaction and Implications

The resignation raised concerns about political stability and prompted several of Mbeki's cabinet ministers, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, to tender their resignations—though Manuel later indicated his willingness to continue serving, helping to calm anxious financial markets.

Observers cautioned that the manner of Mbeki's removal set a significant precedent and highlighted the ANC's dominance over the machinery of state. Nonetheless, the peaceful transfer of power was viewed by many as a demonstration of the resilience of South Africa's democratic institutions.

The developments left Zuma on a clear path toward the presidency, pending the resolution of his remaining legal challenges and the outcome of the next national elections.

---

*Note: These events took place in September 2008. This report reflects the circumstances and context of that period.*

# Political Turmoil Grips South Africa as Mbeki Resigns, Cabinet Members Follow

**JOHANNESBURG** — South Africa entered a period of profound political uncertainty this week as President Thabo Mbeki formally tendered his resignation, triggering a wave of Cabinet departures and exposing deep fractures within the ruling African National Congress that have been building for years.

Mbeki, who had served as the nation's president since 1999, announced his decision to step down after the ANC's National Executive Committee formally requested his resignation. The move came in the aftermath of a controversial court judgment that raised questions about the handling of corruption charges against ANC President Jacob Zuma, Mbeki's chief political rival.

## A Nation Watches

The resignation marks one of the most significant political developments since the end of apartheid and the country's first democratic elections in 1994. For many South Africans, the sight of a sitting president being recalled by his own party underscored the extraordinary power struggle that has consumed the ANC.

Speaking to the nation in a televised address, Mbeki maintained a measured tone, emphasizing his commitment to constitutional order and denying allegations that he had interfered in the judicial process against Zuma.

"I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 52 years," Mbeki said. "I remain a member of the ANC and therefore respect its decisions."

## The Cabinet Exodus

In the hours and days following the announcement, a number of senior government ministers signaled their intention to resign in solidarity with the outgoing president, raising fears of institutional instability at the highest levels of government.

Among the most closely watched was Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, whose stewardship of the economy has been credited with maintaining investor confidence throughout Mbeki's tenure. News of potential resignations sent ripples through financial markets, with the rand experiencing volatility as traders weighed the implications of a leadership vacuum in economic policy.

ANC officials moved quickly to reassure both domestic and international audiences that the transition would be orderly and that the party remained committed to sound economic management and constitutional governance.

## Background: The Zuma Legal Saga

At the heart of the crisis lies the long-running legal battle involving Jacob Zuma, the ANC president who emerged victorious over Mbeki at the party's Polokwane conference in December 2007.

Zuma's legal troubles trace back several years, entangled with a broader arms procurement scandal. His former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted in 2005 on charges of corruption and fraud, a judgment that referenced a corrupt relationship with Zuma. That conviction prompted Mbeki to dismiss Zuma from his post as deputy president, an act that many observers view as the origin of the bitter rivalry between the two men.

Prosecutors subsequently pursued corruption charges against Zuma directly. The case became a lightning rod for factional tensions within the ANC, with Zuma's supporters alleging that the charges were politically motivated—orchestrated, they claimed, to prevent his rise to national leadership.

The immediate catalyst for Mbeki's downfall was a High Court ruling that dismissed the corruption case against Zuma on procedural grounds. In his judgment, the presiding judge made observations suggesting the possibility of political interference in the timing and handling of the prosecution—remarks that Zuma's allies seized upon as vindication.

Though Mbeki has vigorously denied any improper involvement, the ruling provided his opponents within the ANC's National Executive Committee with the leverage needed to demand his recall.

## A Divided Party

The events of September 2008 have laid bare the depth of division within Africa's oldest liberation movement. The Polokwane conference had already signaled a decisive shift, with Zuma's camp capturing key leadership positions and leaving Mbeki increasingly isolated.

Analysts note that the tensions reflect not only personal rivalries but also differing visions for the country's future—debates over economic policy, the pace of transformation, and the distribution of power within the party and state.

"This is a moment of testing for South Africa's democratic institutions," said one political analyst based in Johannesburg. "The manner in which this transition is managed will speak volumes about the maturity of the country's democracy."

## Looking Ahead

With Mbeki's departure, attention now turns to the process of appointing a caretaker leader to guide the country until national elections, widely expected in 2009. The ANC's parliamentary majority means the party will select the interim president, with Zuma himself constitutionally barred from immediately assuming the office as he does not currently hold a parliamentary seat.

The name of Deputy ANC President Kgalema Motlanthe has emerged prominently in discussions as a potential steady hand to steer the country through the transitional period.

For ordinary South Africans, many of whom have grown weary of elite political battles, the hope is that the turbulence at the top will not disrupt the delivery of essential services or derail the nation's hard-won stability.

As the country navigates these uncharted waters, the world watches to see whether South Africa's constitutional framework—forged in the optimism of the post-apartheid transition—will prove resilient enough to absorb the shock of its most serious political crisis in more than a decade.

# South Africa in Political Turmoil as Cabinet Resignations Follow Mbeki's Exit

**Breaking News Analysis**

South Africa is navigating one of its most significant political transitions since the end of apartheid, as the fallout from President Thabo Mbeki's departure sends shockwaves through the government and the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

## Cabinet Resignations Rock Pretoria

In the wake of Mbeki's recall by the ANC, a wave of resignations has raised concerns about political stability and continuity in governance. Among the most consequential departures is that of **Finance Minister Trevor Manuel**, whose stewardship of the national economy earned him considerable respect both domestically and internationally.

Manuel, who served as finance minister for over a decade, became synonymous with fiscal discipline and prudent economic management. His resignation initially triggered anxiety in financial markets, given his role as a stabilizing figure and his credibility with investors. Officials moved quickly to clarify the situation, seeking to reassure markets that his departure would not derail economic policy.

**Mosiuoa "Terror" Lekota**, the Defence Minister and a prominent ANC veteran, also announced his resignation. Lekota, a struggle-era stalwart, has been openly critical of the direction the party has taken, and his departure signals deeper ideological and factional fractures within the ANC.

## The Mbeki Legacy: Achievements and Controversies

Thabo Mbeki's tenure as president was marked by significant accomplishments alongside notable controversies. Under his leadership, South Africa experienced sustained economic growth, with the economy expanding steadily and a growing black middle class emerging.

Key achievements of the Mbeki era include:

- **Economic stability and growth** driven by responsible macroeconomic policies
- **Championing the African Renaissance**, a vision aimed at continental development and unity
- **Playing a prominent role in African diplomacy** and conflict resolution
- **Strengthening South Africa's global standing** as a regional power and voice for the developing world

However, his presidency was not without criticism. His controversial stance on HIV/AIDS, including skepticism toward the link between HIV and AIDS, drew widespread condemnation and was blamed for policy failures that had serious public health consequences. Critics also charged that his leadership style was aloof and centralized.

## The Zuma Rivalry: A Battle for the ANC's Soul

At the heart of Mbeki's downfall lies his protracted and bitter rivalry with **Jacob Zuma**, his former deputy president. The conflict between the two men represented not only a personal power struggle but also competing visions for the future of the ANC and the country.

The rivalry intensified after Mbeki dismissed Zuma from the deputy presidency amid corruption allegations. Zuma's supporters viewed this as a politically motivated attack, and the populist momentum behind him grew. At the ANC's Polokwane conference, Zuma decisively defeated Mbeki for the party leadership, setting the stage for Mbeki's eventual recall.

The tipping point came when a judge's remarks suggested possible political interference in Zuma's corruption case—implications that reflected poorly on the Mbeki administration. Seizing the moment, the ANC's National Executive Committee moved to recall Mbeki, effectively ending his presidency before the completion of his term.

## Mbeki's Diplomatic Role in the Zimbabwe Power-Sharing Deal

Even as domestic political pressures mounted, Mbeki remained deeply engaged in one of the region's most pressing crises: the political impasse in neighboring **Zimbabwe**. As the designated mediator on behalf of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), Mbeki brokered a landmark power-sharing agreement between President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai.

The deal, aimed at ending a deadlock following disputed elections, sought to establish a unity government in which Mugabe would retain the presidency while Tsvangirai assumed the role of prime minister. Mbeki's involvement reflected his broader commitment to African diplomacy and his preference for negotiated settlements.

However, his approach—often characterized as "quiet diplomacy"—drew criticism from those who felt he was too accommodating toward Mugabe and insufficiently firm in addressing the crisis. The durability of the power-sharing arrangement remains uncertain, and Mbeki's departure from office raises questions about the continuity of the mediation process.

## Looking Ahead: Uncertainty and Transition

South Africa now faces a period of transition as the ANC works to install a caretaker leadership to guide the country until the next elections. The resignations of key cabinet members underscore the depth of the divisions within the ruling party and the challenges that lie ahead.

As the nation absorbs these developments, questions loom about the stability of governance, the trajectory of economic policy, and the future direction of a country that remains the economic powerhouse of the African continent. The coming weeks and months will prove critical in determining whether South Africa can navigate this turbulent chapter while preserving the institutional strength and democratic gains achieved since 1994.
